newsitem.title: USA: Testimony in Simpson case centers on 1993 photo.
newsitem.headline: Testimony in Simpson case centers on 1993 photo.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial on Wednesday saw a 1993 photograph of the former football star wearing shoes that the plaintiffs' attorneys contend link him to the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

The picture, taken by freelance photographer Harry Scull during a football game, was never introduced as evidence in Simpson's criminal trial but was published in March of this year in the National Enquirer.
Scull, whose testimony was introduced to the jury by videotape and through transcripts, admitted selling the picture to the tabloid for $5,000.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of criminal charges in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. He is currently battling a wrongful death lawsuit filed by families of the victims, who are seeking financial damages.

During the criminal trial, FBI shoe-print expert William Bodziak testified that bloody shoe prints found at the crime scene could be traced to a specific size and brand, size 12 Bruno Maglis. Simpson has denied ever owning the shoes.
Lawyers for the victims' families are expected to call Bodziak to the witness stand to testify that Scull's photo shows Simpson wearing the Bruno Magli shoes.
Scull testified on Wednesday that he took the picture of Simpson, who was working as a television commentator, before the start of a football game in Buffalo, New York.

Scull said he sent the photo to Pro Football Weekly magazine about one week after the game but kept the negative. It wasn't until June 1995, during Simpson's criminal trial, that he remembered the picture again and offered it to the National Enquirer, he said.

Simpson's attorneys used their cross-examination of Scull to suggest the picture had been doctored. Scull said the photograph had been sent to London and scanned into a computer for a photo agency, but answered "absolutely not" when asked if he had altered the picture.
Earlier on Wednesday, jurors watched a videotape of Simpson struggling to pull on a pair of bloody gloves during a pivotal moment in his criminal trial.

In the video from June 15, 1995, Simpson was seen having trouble fitting into the brown leather gloves, one discovered on his property and the other found near the bodies at Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium.
Prosecutors in the criminal case argued that the gloves were dropped by the killer. The defence claimed the glove found at Simpson's home was planted by the police.

The seemingly bad fit of the gloves during the demonstration was later cited by Simpson's criminal defence attorney, Johnnie Cochran, who told jurors during his closing arguments in that case, "If it does not fit, you must acquit."
Wednesday's replay of the now-famous glove demonstration came during the testimony of Richard Rubin, the same witness who was on the stand when prosecutors asked Simpson to try on the gloves.

The plaintiffs' attorneys called Rubin, a former vice-president for the Aris glove company, to testify the two gloves were a pair manufactured in limited quantity before 1992 and sold exclusively to Bloomingdales department store.
Brown family attorney John Kelly then showed Rubin a series of pictures taken prior to the murders depicting Simpson wearing leather gloves as he provided television commentary during football games.

Rubin testified the gloves seen in the photos were the same brand and style as those found at the murder scene and at Simpson's home. The families' attorneys claim Nicole Brown Simpson purchased two pair of the gloves, called Aris Leather Lights, on Dec. 18, 1990.
